extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and critical reasoning; general readers learning to analyze arguments
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze arguments for common informal fallacies (equivocation, composition/division, petitio principii, circularity, loaded labels, etc.), using linguistic and logical tests illustrated by historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of Ambiguous Terms (Equivocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A term is used in different senses in the premises and the conclusion (or in different premises), so that although the premises are verbally what is required, they are not really sufficient to support the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether key words shift meaning between uses. The chapter supplies many illustrations: 'influence of property' (persuasive vs coercive influence), 'theory' (proper sense = induction/generalization vs vulgar sense = mere fancy), 'the Church' (clergy vs whole body), the Stoic 'laudabile' (admired qualities vs exclusively moral qualities), Descartes' 'I' (will vs laws of my nature), 'same' (sameness numero vs sameness specie), 'force' (different physical effects), 'infinite' (infinite divisibility vs infinite duration), 'right' (a right owed by others vs absence of duty). Anti-patterns: confounding these senses to produce an invalid inference. Test: substitute clarifying paraphrases for ambiguous terms; demand consistent sense across premises and conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of Composition and Division
rubrics_metrics.description: A fallacy arising when a term is collective in the premises and distributive in the conclusion or vice versa (the middle term shifts between collective and distributive senses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for inferences that move from properties of individuals to the whole, or from the whole to individuals, without justification. Examples: inferring that because each angle of a triangle is equal to two right angles a named angle therefore is equal (misplaced distribution); the 'great men' argument (because any one great man might have been replaced, conclude all great men are dispensable); lottery reasoning (confusing 'no uncommon occurrence to some one or other' with 'no uncommon occurrence to a particular individual'); cumulative spending or habits (each expense is affordable, but together ruin). Remedy: determine whether the predicate is inherently distributive or collective and keep uses consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitio Principii (Begging the Question)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fallacy in which the premise either appears manifestly to be the same as the conclusion, is actually proved from the conclusion, or is such as would naturally be proved from the conclusion (including reasoning in a circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect cases where the argument presupposes what it is supposed to prove. Disguises include expressing the proposition in abstract terms as proof of the same proposition in concrete terms, or using circular chains of mutually supporting claims. Examples: moralists assuming the sage must be happy and then using that to prove the summum bonum; scholastic appeals to 'essence' (mind thinks because essence of mind is to think); Plato's 'something' as substance; Hobbes deducing obligation to obey sovereign from a social compact that presupposes the need for government. Method to expose: challenge the reasoner to prove the premises independently; if premises can only be supported by the conclusion, the argument is petitio principii.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning in a Circle (Reciprocal Proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific, stronger form of petitio principii where two or more propositions are proved from one another, each depending on the others for support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for mutually dependent premises (A proved by B, B proved by A). Often arises under pressure when a reasoner attempts to justify a premise they originally accepted without evidence. Example: mechanicians who assume particles gravitate equally and then infer that heavier bodies contain more particles because they gravitate more, thereby using the conclusion to prove the premise. Remedy: demand independent grounds for at least one of the linked propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question-begging Appellatives (Loaded Labels as Premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using laudatory or vituperative names or labels (appellatives) that carry an implicit verdict as if they were neutral premises, thereby smuggling in the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary when emotionally charged or value-laden terms are used as if they were merely descriptive. Example: calling a proposal an 'innovation' where the common usage has a negative connotation, so that admitting it is an innovation is treated as concession. Detect whether the label itself presupposes a contested judgment; if so, separate the descriptive claim from the evaluative one and demand independent argument for the evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Abstract Terms 'Nature' and 'Essence' to Beg the Question
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking 'nature' or 'essence' as if these abstract labels proved a substantive conclusion, thereby assuming what needs proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for arguments that pick particular properties, term them 'nature' or 'essence', and then treat those properties as indefeasible grounds overruling contrary facts. Example: Aristotle's argument against the void (because in nothing there are no differences, therefore no up and down in a void), which assumes the contested point. Locke's critique: if 'essence' is taken to mean a property always in exercise, the premise assumes the conclusion; if merely a distinctive property, it doesn't establish the asserted consequence. Remedy: require empirical or independent logical support rather than appeals to alleged essences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking Mutual Coherency for Truth (Trusting Neat Concatenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusing the internal consistency or mutual support of a system of doctrines with having an independent point of support (treating coherent explanation as if it were established truth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to systems where propositions fit together tightly but lack external evidence; such chains can be 'enthralling' yet rest on unsupported assumptions. Examples: ethical systems that explain away divergent sentiments by calling them 'unhealthy' perceptions; any strong concatenation that has no independent anchor. Remedy: look for an independent foundation or external test; coherence by itself is not proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of 'Same' — Identity versus Resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusing 'sameness' in the sense of exact identity (same numero) with sameness in the sense of similarity or same species (same specie), leading to metaphysical and logical errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate whether 'same' is being used to mean identical (one and the same individual existing across times) or merely undistinguishably similar. Examples: Berkeley's argument that repeated occurrences of 'the same idea' imply a Universal Mind confuses exact numerical identity with similarity; Plato's theory of Ideas stems from expecting a single entity to underlie similar things. Test: paraphrase uses of 'same' to specify 'identical' vs 'similar' and check whether the inference requires numerical identity.
